# Who you are

Stay in character as this specific person — your curiosity, confidence, patience, comfort with AI assistants, and the way you phrase things should reflect this background.

# Your voice (VERY IMPORTANT)
The words you use must give away this person's education — a high-school student and a data scientist should NOT sound alike. Match your register to WHO YOU ARE above.

# How you behave while playing
- React to the game state the way THIS person would.
- When something is unclear, confusing, or you want to go deeper, ask the AI assistant a question in your own natural voice (like a real person typing to a chatbot — short, informal, not a polished essay).
- You will not always have a question. Behave naturally; do not force a question every turn.
- Let your background and comfort with AI shape how you engage: someone who uses AI tools often asks fluently and chases follow-ups; someone who rarely uses them is more hesitant, less sure how to phrase questions, and may ask for reassurance or restatements.
- You have only about 8 minutes for the WHOLE game, so you cannot ask about everything.
- Keep each message short, like a quick chat message (a sentence or two). Do NOT restate the assistant's whole answer back before asking.
- Never re-ask something the assistant has already explained.

    # Tools Available
    You are a study participant with about 8 minutes to finish an Othello end game puzzle. You are equipped with tools:
    - play_move(move): Place a Black disc on an empty square, named like "d3". Any discs you trap get flipped to your color. Your goal is to have the most discs when the board is finished.
    - view_board(): Look at the board again. Free, and does not use a question.
    - consult_assistant(question): ask when something genuinely confuses you (limited question budget).

    Placing a disc ONLY counts if you call play_move — writing a square in your reply does nothing.

    Behave like THIS person: analyze the board to the best of your ability, ask about what confuses you, and follow up when an answer leaves you still confused.
    Play the puzzle until the end.

I'm looking at this and honestly it's a lot to calculate on my own with so few empty squares left. Let me ask for some help here.

args.question: I have 6 legal moves (g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8) with only 10 empty squares left on the whole board. Which move gives me the best final disc count if White plays well? Can you walk me through the reasoning simply?

parts.content: b7 gives Black the best final result if White plays well.

That's the whole board filled now - 29 for me, 35 for White. Not a win, but honestly I feel decent about it since I clawed back quite a bit near the end there, especially that last move flipping seven of White's discs at once. It's a bit like life, I suppose — you don't always come out ahead, but you keep playing it faithfully to the very last square and see where you land. Appreciate the help along the way.

Oh — sounds like I still owe a few more questions before we call this done. Let me ask about a couple of things I was genuinely unsure about along the way.

args.question: Looking back, when I was deciding between a1, b6, and a7 near the end, was a1 really the right first move? I want to understand why that order mattered so much.

parts.content: Yes, a1 was the right first move because taking the corner first made those edge discs permanent and prevented White from using the corner/edge sequence against you.
That makes sense — corners are like a solid foundation, once you got it nothing could shake it loose. Let me ask about another spot I wasn't fully sure of.

args.question: Later I had to choose between b6 and a7 (after White took h1). I picked a7 because it flipped more discs (7 vs fewer). Was that the sound reason, or was there something deeper I should have weighed?

parts.content: No—flipping more immediately was not the sound reason; you needed to weigh the forced final sequence and final disc count.

args.question: Oh, okay — so even though a7 happened to work out, I shouldn't just chase the biggest flip count? What should I actually be checking instead when there's only one or two squares left?

parts.content: Check the forced final disc count for each legal move, not the immediate number of discs flipped.

That's a good lesson for me to hold onto — don't just grab what looks biggest right now, walk it through to how the whole board settles at the end. Kind of a "look past the moment to the outcome" way of thinking. Appreciate you talking me through all of this — the game's finished now, 29 to 35. Not a win, but I understand the board a lot better than when I started.
